The Book of EnoEdward L. Betz Jr.

Why manuscripts stall

A good idea can still read like a first draft.

Readers forgive a lot. They don’t forgive a book that feels unfinished.

  • The same idea, told again

    A point you love lands three times in almost the same words, so by the third time it no longer surprises anyone. I map where each idea works hardest and let later chapters build on it.

  • Habits of phrasing

    In one sample manuscript, “I began” appeared 25 times in about 100 pages. Small habits like that make a voice feel tired. I find them and vary them.

  • Pacing that loses readers

    A slow opening, an early reveal, or an explanation that arrives before the story has earned it. I read as a reader first, so I can tell you where attention drops.

  • Small slips that signal “unfinished”

    A missing full stop, a contents page that does not match the chapters, an unnamed copyright holder. Readers and reviewers notice these in the first pages.

What I do

Editing, from the big picture down to the last comma.

Big issues first, polish last. You never pay to perfect a paragraph that later gets cut.

Developmental editing

The big picture: structure, pacing, argument, characters, repetition and gaps. Best for new drafts and manuscripts that feel almost there.

You getAn editorial letter with chapter-by-chapter notes, and a clear order for your revisions.

Line editing

Clarity, rhythm and tightening at sentence level. I sharpen your voice instead of replacing it.

You getTracked changes with a short reason beside each one, so your next chapter starts cleaner.

Copyediting

Grammar, spelling, punctuation and consistency of style, including hedges and look-alike headings that confuse readers.

You getA clean manuscript with consistent style, and questions flagged for you instead of guesses.

Proofreading

The last look before you print or upload: typos, contents page, copyright page, front-matter slips.

You getA publication-ready file you can send out with confidence.

Manuscript assessment and beta reading

An honest read of part or all of your book, as a reader first and an editor second. Fiction or nonfiction, with the right checklist for each.

You getA written report with strengths, risks, line-level suggestions and a ranked revision plan.

Book cover design

Front, spine and back designed as one wrap, with print specs and mockups ready for your launch. The cover promises what the editing delivers.

Interior design and formatting

Title page, contents, chapter openers and page numbers, prepared for Kindle and print on Amazon KDP.

How it works

You see my work before you commit to anything.

  1. Send your first 500 words

    By email or WhatsApp, with a line about your book and your goal for it.

  2. Get your free sample edit

    I edit those 500 words with tracked changes and a comment explaining each change. You judge my eye and my respect for your voice. No obligation.

  3. Share the details for a quote

    Tell me the word count, genre, formats you need and your launch date. I recommend the right level of editing and quote from there.

  4. Big issues first

    A developmental read comes before any polish, so structure and repetition are fixed while changes are still cheap.

  5. Line edit and copyedit

    Tracked changes, each with a reason. Where I need your input, such as a missing name or an unfinished sentence, I ask instead of guessing.

  6. Proofread and prepare to publish

    A final check, then a publication-ready file. If you need a cover or interior layout, it comes from the same hands.

What I need for a quote

  • Word count
  • Genre
  • Formats you need (Kindle, paperback, hardcover)
  • Your launch date

Edits in action

This is what a comment from me looks like.

Every change comes with what I changed, why, and what it does for your book. Pick an example and switch between the original, my version and the tracked changes.

Once I had taken the first step, I discovered that learning a skill was not going to be as simple as I had imagined. There were things I understood quickly and others that required much more patience. There were days when I felt like I was making progress and other days when I questioned whether I was improving at all.

Once I took that first step, I found that learning a skill was harder than I had imagined. Some things came quickly; others demanded patience. On some days I felt I was making progress; on others I wondered whether I was improving at all.

Chapter 4, opening paragraph. 60 words became 44, with every idea kept.

Editor’s comment to the authorThis opening carries the chapter’s emotional shift from excitement to difficulty, so it should move briskly. Your “There were… There were…” pair is accurate but slow. A paired “some / others” shows the same ups and downs in half the space.
What I changed
Turned “not going to be as simple as” into “harder than”, “discovered” into “found”, and joined the two contrasts into parallel “some / others” and “on some days / on others” pairs.
Why
Negative phrasing and a repeated “There were” make the reader decode before they feel. Positive, parallel phrasing lets them feel the struggle straight away.
Result for the author
About 27% shorter with every idea intact. The chapter’s turning point arrives faster and reads with more energy.

Chapter 1: “I began to understand that confidence often comes after action, not before it.”

Chapter 3: “You may wait for confidence, but sometimes confidence comes because you started.”

Chapter 7: “You do not always need confidence to take action. Sometimes action creates confidence.”

Chapter 1 plants it. Keep the line exactly as written.

Chapter 3 shows the fear of starting. Keep the story, cut the restatement.

Chapter 7 proves it with one real moment from the author’s own learning.

Chapters 1, 3 and 7. One idea, three jobs, instead of one idea told three times.

Editor’s comment to the authorThis is the strongest idea in your book, and readers will remember it. But they meet it three times in almost the same words, so by Chapter 7 it no longer surprises them. I’d keep each idea where it works hardest and let later chapters build on it.
What I changed
Gave each chapter a different job for the idea instead of restating it, and left a marked spot for a true story only the author can tell.
Why
When readers feel they have heard a point already, they skim, and a skimmed chapter can’t change anyone. A concrete moment also makes advice believable.
Result for the author
Tighter chapters, a stronger Chapter 7, and a reader who feels the idea instead of re-reading it.

Front matter: contents page and copyright page. Three small slips, and one question I could not answer for you.

Editor’s comment to the authorThe first pages decide how carefully a reader, or a reviewer, expects the rest to be made. Three things to settle before this goes to print. For the last one I need your input: which name should appear as the copyright holder?
What I changed
Pluralised the contents heading, added the missing full stop, and flagged the copyright line as a question rather than guessing a name.
Why
The page lists many chapters, so the heading takes the plural. A sentence needs its full stop. A copyright notice should name who owns the copyright.
Result for the author
A book that gives no one a reason to doubt it at first glance, and one open question settled before printing.

About me

Hi, I’m Tijani Uthman.

I’m a book editor with nine years of experience, helping self-publishing authors turn drafts into books they’re proud to put their name on.

Editing is my main work: developmental, line and copy editing, proofreading and manuscript assessment. I also design covers and interiors, so the promise on the cover matches what’s inside.

I work with authors in the United States and Nigeria, by email and WhatsApp, and I can help whether you are publishing for the first time or the fifth.

My rule is simple. I tighten and clarify. I don’t rewrite you.

Your voice stays yours

Lines that carry your personality are left exactly as written, and I tell you which ones.

Every change is explained

Each edit comes with a comment and a reason, so you learn the pattern.

Honest, specific feedback

Where I need your input, I flag it as a question instead of guessing.

One person, one process

Editing and design come from the same hands, so nothing gets lost in a handoff.

Questions

Answers before you reach out.

How does the free sample edit work?
Send the first 500 words of your manuscript by email or WhatsApp. I edit them with tracked changes and a comment explaining each change, then send them back. There is no cost and no obligation.
Which type of editing do I need?
If the draft is new, or feels almost there, start with developmental editing. If the structure is settled, a line edit and copyedit polish the sentences. A proofread is the last check before you print or upload. Not sure? Send your sample and I will tell you honestly.
Will you change my voice?
No. I tighten and clarify; I don’t rewrite you. The lines that carry your personality are left exactly as written, and I tell you which ones.
What will I receive?
It depends on the service. A developmental edit comes as an editorial letter with chapter-by-chapter notes. A line edit comes as tracked changes with a reason beside each one. A copyedit gives you a clean manuscript with consistent style. An assessment or beta read comes as a written report with a ranked revision plan.
What do you need to give me a quote?
Your word count, genre, the formats you need (Kindle, paperback or hardcover) and your launch date.
How long will it take?
It depends on the length of your book and the type of editing. After I have seen your sample and your word count, I confirm a realistic timeline before we start.
Where are your clients based?
I work with authors in the United States and Nigeria, remotely, by email and WhatsApp.
What kinds of books do you edit?
Fiction, nonfiction and business books, memoir and personal growth, children’s books and academic writing. My projects above include a Christian novel, a bilingual picture book, a technology-and-society title and a personal memoir.
Can you also design my cover and format my book?
Yes. Editing is my main service, but I also design covers (front, spine and back as one wrap) and format interiors for Kindle and print on Amazon KDP. Doing both means the promise on the cover matches what’s inside.
Can I hire you through Upwork?
Yes. You can contact me directly using the form above, or hire me through my Upwork profile.
